Diana Colella to Lead Autodesk's AEC Division, Promising Deeper AI Integrations
Former media and entertainment division head aims to further link the Forma design cloud platform into artificial intelligence workflows
By Jeff Yoders, Senior Editor, Technology
Autodesk's Forma cloud platform has become connected data layer for all of Autodesk's architecture and construction products.
Autodesk announced Oct. 6 that Diana Colella will be the new executive vice president of the San Francisco software giant's architecture, engineering and construction business unit.
Colella succeeds Amy Bunszel, who announced her retirement in August and will stay with Autodesk through November 2 to support the transition.
Colella will lead Autodesk’s largest industry business as the company enters a new phase of what it says is growth in AEC, driven by Autodesk Forma, the company’s industry cloud for AEC that connects data, context and design and construction workflows. Like Bunszel, Colella will have to shepherd the fusion of Autodesk's artificial intelligence and project intelligence efforts into the AEC project lifecycle.
Autodesk said in its announcement that Colella, most recently the head of the company's media and entertainment division and with nearly three decades at Autodesk, will work to advance the Forma strategy while continuing to evolve Autodesk's desktop products such as Revit and Civil 3D and connect them more closely to Forma workflows.
In an internal email to all employees, Autodesk CEO and President Andrew Anagnost said, "Diana is also an internal disruptor and challenger who is willing to question how we’ve always done things while staying close to customers. In M&E, she revamped a portfolio of standalone products into a connected platform strategy through Flow [Autodesk's cloud platform for the media and entertainment industries]."
Colella joined Autodesk more than 29 years ago via the acquisition of Discreet Logic and has since held leadership roles including leading Autodesk’s AutoCAD business and helping launch One AutoCAD. She also previously worked for KPMG, is a certified public accountant and holds a master's degree from McGill University. She is known for openly communicating with customers through Autodesk's regular sales channels but also at public events such as its annual Autodesk University user conference.
Anagnost said in his company email that Colella's mandate is to accelerate the embedding of AI in critical workflows and strengthen the execution of those integrations across the full AEC lifecycle.
"Our customers are being asked to deliver more while navigating greater complexity, persistent resource constraints and rapid technological change," Colella said in a statement. "My priority is to listen to them, build on the strong foundation Amy and the team have created, and make sure the work we’re doing across Forma and AI translates into meaningful improvements in how projects are designed, built and operated."

Autodesk's real bet at AU 2026 isn't a product. It's an assistant that knows the project
Every AI story at Autodesk University this year eventually comes back to the same argument: capacity, not ideas, is the constraint holding architecture, engineering, construction, manufacturing, and entertainment back. Especially if you look at the Australian stats from the State of Design and Make report. CEO Andrew Anagnost has been making that case for two years running. What is new at AU 2026 is the thing Autodesk is pointing to as the mechanism for unlocking it, the next generation of Autodesk Assistant.
If you have used Autodesk software recently, you've already met an earlier version of Assistant, a conversational helper sitting inside Fusion, Forma or Flow, answering questions, and taking a few tasks off your plate. That version is still there, and it is not going anywhere. What Autodesk previewed this week is something more ambitious, an agentic AI experience designed to work across products, projects, and teams rather than staying locked inside whichever tool you happen to have open.
Why this is not just another chatbot It's worth being precise about what "agentic" means here because the word gets thrown around loosely. Autodesk's definition is AI that uses project context to help professionals understand, plan and take action toward an intended outcome, not simply answer a question.
In practice, that is the difference between an assistant you have to ask the right question, and one that already knows something needs your attention before you have thought to ask. Anagnost frames the underlying problem plainly: "The constraint in our industries has never been about ideas. It is capacity, and the next generation of Autodesk Assistant delivers project intelligence to unlock more of it. For Design and Make professionals, 'probably right' is wrong because their work has consequences in the real world."
That last line is doing a lot of work. A general-purpose AI model can reason across anything, but it does not know your building code, your manufacturing tolerances, your production schedule, or the history of decisions that got a project to where it is today. Autodesk's pitch is that its Assistant does, because it's grounded in what the company calls project intelligence: actionable insight built from connected project data, industry context, and more than four decades of Autodesk's own design and engineering expertise, not the open internet.
Three industry clouds, one intelligence layer The next-generation Assistant isn't a standalone product bolted onto Autodesk's existing tools. It sits across the company's three industry clouds, each connecting a different part of the design-and-build world:
Autodesk Forma: the industry cloud for architecture, engineering and construction, bringing planning, design, construction and operations data into one connected environment.
Autodesk Fusion: the industry cloud for design and manufacturing, connecting product design, engineering, manufacturing and production around shared product data.
Autodesk Flow: the industry cloud for media and entertainment, connecting creative teams, production data and AI across content creation.
Because Assistant draws on all three, it can follow a problem across boundaries that used to require a person to manually reconstruct context every time work moved from one team or tool to the next. Autodesk's own example is a structural change to a building: the next generation of Assistant can understand what that change affects downstream, fabrication, schedule, cost, construction sequencing, operations, and surface the specific Autodesk capabilities needed to deal with it, rather than just describing that a problem exists.
Marius Jablonskis, Digital Transformation Leader at Norconsult, put his finger on why that matters to an actual project team: "Project teams don't work in one tool or one part of a project, and the next generation of Autodesk Assistant reflects that. The potential is to bring the right project context into the workflow so teams can understand what needs attention and act on it more easily. We also see real value in being able to bring our own tools and intelligence into the experience alongside Autodesk's."
What it actually does Strip away the branding and the next-generation Assistant is built around three concrete priorities:
Understand what needs attention. Personal Pulse surfaces prioritised issues and insights across a person's project, so the things that matter do not get buried in a task list. Assistant Spaces gives teams, and their own AI agents, a focused environment to investigate a specific problem together and see its downstream effects before committing to a decision.
Act across workflows. Assistant brings Autodesk's specialised design, engineering, and creative AI together with the precise tools professionals already rely on, turning intent into a reviewable outcome through natural language or voice, rather than requiring someone to manually operate five different pieces of software to get there.
Bring your own intelligence. Assistant Builder lets customers connect their own AI agents, tools and trusted partner services directly into Autodesk's project context, with support planned for third-party agents through the new Design & Make Marketplace. Autodesk is not pretending it can build every capability a customer needs. Instead, it is positioning itself as the connective layer other tools plug into.
Behind all of it is the Autodesk AI Orchestrator, which chooses between different AI models for a given task based on accuracy, speed, security, and cost, rather than routing every problem through a single model. It is a quietly significant design choice: Autodesk is betting that no one model will ever be the right answer for everything from a natural-language site query to a structural engineering calculation, so the system picks its intelligence to fit the job.
What this looks like industry by industry Architecture, engineering, and construction. Inside Forma and Revit, Assistant helps architects explore more design options and cuts down on repetitive documentation work, while flagging project changes that need human attention rather than burying them in a drawing set. New AI-powered construction agents handle document search, submittal review, and bid processing, reducing the manual review load on already-stretched project teams.
Design and manufacturing. In Fusion, new AI capabilities automate repetitive design and manufacturing tasks, and a new agentic PLM (product lifecycle management) experience helps connect product data and decisions across teams who would otherwise be working from different versions of the truth. Assistant is also expanding into Inventor and Vault, meeting engineers inside the tools they already use daily rather than asking them to adopt something new.
Media and entertainment. In Flow, tools like Flow Studio let artists assemble characters and AI-generated worlds and then direct and refine them in an editable 3D environment, keeping creative control with the artist rather than handing it to the model. MotionMaker in Maya reduces repetitive animation work while leaving the final performance in human hands.
Operations. With MaintainX now part of Autodesk, the operational data an asset generates after it's built, equipment performance, maintenance history, failure patterns, can feed back into Assistant and inform not just how that asset is maintained, but how the next one is designed. It is the clearest expression of Autodesk's "closing the loop" idea: intelligence that does not stop accumulating the day a project is handed over.
The trust question, and the honest caveats None of this works if nobody trusts the output, and Autodesk is clearly aware of that. Every Autodesk AI capability, including Assistant, is evaluated for data integrity, privacy and risk, and the company publishes AI Transparency Cards covering the data and technologies behind Assistant, its safeguards, and its known limitations. Assistant is explicitly designed to support professional judgment rather than replace it, with human oversight built in rather than optional.
It is also worth being clear-eyed about timing. Autodesk Assistant itself is available today across many Autodesk products, including Fusion, Forma and Flow. The next-generation, cross-product experience being previewed at AU 2026 is not yet generally available. Availability, rollout timing, subscription terms, and regional details are slated to be announced in 2027. This is a preview of direction, not a shipped product sitting on every desktop next week.
Why it matters beyond the keynote stage Autodesk's own 2027 State of Design & Make Report found that 70% of Design and Make leaders and experts surveyed expect AI to reduce mundane and repetitive work and free up capacity for the judgment, creativity, and ability their work requires. That is a consistent read across the industries Autodesk serves: professionals are not looking for AI to make the creative or technical calls. They are looking for it to clear away everything standing between them and making those calls well.
That is the real story behind the next generation of Autodesk Assistant. It is not a smarter chatbot. Adobe (ADBE) vs. Autodesk (ADSK): Which AI-Hit Software Stock Has the Better Comeback?
Mon, October 5, 2026 at 8:48 PM PDT 5 min read
Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) and Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK) have something unusual in common. Both are excellent software companies that have been punished by investors for fears that artificial intelligence could make their products less valuable.
But the threat is not really the same.
Adobe's biggest problem is that AI can make it dramatically easier to create images, videos, designs, and documents. Some of the work that once required expensive professional software can now be done with a prompt.
Autodesk faces a different situation. Its software helps engineers, architects, manufacturers, and construction companies design things that eventually have to exist in the real world. AI can make those workflows faster, but it does not eliminate the need for precise engineering software.
Adobe ranks last in our list of 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. To see which stocks outranked it, click HERE.
Adobe (ADBE) vs. Autodesk (ADSK): Which AI-Hit Software Stock Has the Better Comeback?
Adobe has to prove that AI is a growth story, not a disruption story
Adobe's business is still remarkably strong.
Revenue grew 12% year over year in its latest quarter, while subscription revenue grew 14%. Adobe also crossed 1 billion monthly active users across its products. More importantly, its AI-first annual recurring revenue, or recurring revenue tied directly to newer AI products, surpassed $650 million and grew more than 150%.
The problem is that investors aren't convinced yet.
Adobe is increasingly giving users free access to products such as Firefly and Express in an effort to attract a much larger audience. That has helped push its creative freemium user base above 100 million, but it also means some users who might once have paid Adobe are now entering through a free funnel. Management expects the monetization of those users to show up later.
That is a risky bet. Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) needs AI to increase the value of its ecosystem faster than it reduces the value of the underlying software.
DON'T MISS: 12 High-Flying Stocks to Invest In
There are encouraging signs. Firefly, Adobe's generative AI platform, is being embedded into Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud products. Adobe is also building AI agents that can handle repetitive creative and marketing tasks rather than simply generate an image or paragraph.
But competitors are coming from every direction, from AI startups to cheaper creative tools. That is why the market has become so skeptical despite Adobe continuing to grow.
Autodesk's AI story is less flashy, but I think it may be easier to defend.
The company's software sits inside architecture, engineering, construction, and manufacturing workflows. These aren't just creative outputs. They are buildings, factories, machines and infrastructure.
That gives Autodesk something many AI companies do not have: context.
Autodesk is trying to connect design, construction, manufacturing and operations into one continuous flow of information. Its recent $3.6 billion acquisition of MaintainX is part of that strategy, bringing maintenance and operational data into the platform.
If Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK) knows how something was designed, how it was built, and eventually how it performs in the real world, AI has much more useful information to work with.
Management calls this "project intelligence." In simpler terms, Autodesk wants to understand the entire life of an asset rather than just the design stage.
That could become a genuine competitive advantage.
The company's latest quarter showed that this isn't just an AI story on a slide. Revenue grew 16%, operating margins expanded, and management raised its full-year outlook.
So which stock is the better comeback?
This is where the valuation changes the answer.
Adobe is clearly the cheaper stock. At 8.73x forward earnings, the market is already assuming that its growth will slow and that AI will put pressure on its traditional businesses.
Autodesk at 17.61x is asking investors to pay more for a company whose AI strategy arguably has fewer obvious ways to undermine its core franchise.
Autodesk's business story looks like a more compelling case.
The more complicated the physical world becomes, the more valuable precise design, engineering, and operational data could become. Autodesk is trying to make that data more useful with AI, rather than simply defending software against AI-generated alternatives. Its management argues that the combination of industry data, context and engineering expertise can create an advantage that gets stronger as more workflows connect.
Adobe has a much harder job. It has to convince investors that AI will expand the creative economy enough to offset the possibility that AI also makes creative software easier to replace.
That said, Adobe shouldn't be dismissed at this valuation.
If its free users eventually convert into paying customers, while Firefly, Acrobat AI and its enterprise AI products become meaningful sources of incremental revenue, 8.73x forward earnings could look almost absurdly cheap in hindsight.
Adobe is much cheaper, but that alone does not make it the better buy. Autodesk trades at 17.61x forward earnings, which does not look expensive if its AI strategy and broader platform start paying off. Adobe has more room for upside if AI turns out to strengthen its business, but Autodesk may have the stronger position to defend.
According to Insider Monkey's database, 81 hedge funds held Adobe in Q2, down from 86 in Q1, while the value of their positions fell from about $5.70 billion to $4.14 billion. Autodesk saw a sharper decline in ownership, with 51 hedge funds holding the stock in Q2 versus 67 in Q1. The value of those positions also dropped from $3.17 billion to $2.28 billion.

How Low Can Autodesk (ADSK) Stock Go?
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 11:44 AM PDT 3 min read
Autodesk (ADSK) stock has lost 22% over the past month following its recent earnings release, outstripping declines in peers such as Bentley Systems (down 16.4%) while the S&P 500 barely moved. If you own the shares, the worry now is a market-wide sell-off landing on top of that loss. So how low could Autodesk stock go if the whole market turns?
Autodesk Stock Has Usually Fallen Further Than The Market
In past market shocks, Autodesk stock has usually fallen further than the S&P 500. Autodesk stock has traded through 15 such shocks since 2007. On average, the stock fell 24.9% from peak to trough during each shock, compared to 15.8% for the index.
Its deepest fall came in the 2008-2009 financial crisis. The stock lost 77% then, against 53% for the S&P 500. No fall in its full price history has been deeper. In the 2022 inflation shock, as the Fed raised rates, the stock fell 42%, against 24% for the index.
After each fall, the stock took a median of 2.7 months to climb from its low back to its old high. Two recoveries took more than a year, though. After the 2022 fall, the stock needed 28 months to return. Autodesk has changed a great deal in the past five years.
How Has Autodesk Changed In Five Years?
Autodesk is now a larger and more profitable business. Its debt is low. Its revenue over the past twelve months was $7.8 billion, against $4.0 billion five years earlier. Autodesk's debt equals 8.7% of its market value, against 20.7% for the S&P 500.
Its operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, has risen every year for three years. It now stands at 27.9%, up from 19.4% three years ago. That is its highest level in ten years.
Autodesk's sales depend heavily on one part of the business. Its largest reported segment, Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations, brought in $3.6 billion in fiscal 2026. That was half of all revenue that year.
Management said on the fiscal Q2 2027 call that its construction business, part of that segment, is growing by more than 20%. Management also said that growth comes from how little the construction industry uses technology, not from cyclical macroeconomic indicators. Management built its outlook on the economy staying broadly stable through the year.
How Much Could Autodesk Alone Cost Your Portfolio?
Suppose your Autodesk shares are a tenth of your portfolio. Now picture the stock falling 77% from today's price, as deep as its 2008-2009 fall. On its own, that holding would take 7.7% off your whole portfolio, with everything else held flat. At a fifth of your portfolio, they would take 15.4%. The wait could be long, too. After the 2009 low, the stock took 58 months to get back to its old high.
You would need to sit through that wait as well as the loss. Whether Autodesk avoids another severe drawdown will depend heavily on whether construction software adoption can truly outpace an economic downturn, rather than slowing with it.

A fall that fast pulls you toward buying, but the shares still cost more than the market on earnings. The reason to buy is that past Autodesk drops this deep mostly paid off, and the business is still sound.
Why Did Autodesk Stock Fall After A Strong Quarter?
News reports tie the start of the fall to a profit outlook that disappointed, even though the quarter itself beat. The shares peaked on August 27, the day Autodesk reported its fiscal second-quarter results. Revenue and earnings per share both came in above the top of management's own guide.
Those reports said investors focused instead on a third-quarter adjusted profit forecast below Wall Street's estimates. Reuters added that investors worry about possible disruption from AI tools.
Autodesk's own price history shows how earlier drops like this one ended. Here, a dip means a fall of 20% or more within 30 trading days. For example, a $100 share that slides to $80 inside that window would count. Autodesk's latest fall is as deep as the drops in that record, so the record applies here.
Autodesk Dip Buyers Mostly Came Out Ahead
Most buyers of past Autodesk dips were ahead a year later. Not counting this drop, the stock had 11 dips since 2010, though the latest two are too recent to judge. Of the other nine, 7 ended the following year higher. The median return over that year was 26%, so half did better and half did worse.
Collecting that gain meant sitting through more losses first. After past dips, the stock fell a median of a further 12% before it turned. The median best gain within the year was 51%. It took a median of 307 days, about ten months, to get there.
Those results come from Autodesk's past, so they only help if the company under today's drop is still in good shape.
Is Autodesk's Business Still Sound Under The Drop?
Autodesk's business is sound, but you still pay more than the market for it. Revenue grew 17.9% over the past twelve months, faster than its three-year average of 14.4% a year. Its largest segment, Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations, grew 22% in fiscal 2026.
Autodesk also keeps more of each sale than the market as a whole. Its operating margin, the share of revenue left after its costs, was 28%, against 18.6% for the S&P 500. Operating cash flow came to 37% of revenue over the past year.
The price is the catch. Autodesk trades at 33.1 times its past year's earnings, against 22.1 for the S&P 500. So you pay about 50% more for each dollar of Autodesk's profit than for the market's.
Profit is also where the one complication shows up. In August, management raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook, which now includes MaintainX, a company Autodesk has already acquired. Management also lowered its guide for the operating margin under standard accounting to 25% to 27%, from 27%. Management said the MaintainX acquisition dilutes margins.
Autodesk's next report is expected in late November. For the fiscal third quarter, management guided adjusted earnings per share of $3.04 to $3.09.
The reason to buy Autodesk now needs the record to repeat and the business to hold up. Adjusted earnings per share below that range in November would break the business half of it. Autodesk Previews Next-Generation Agentic AI Across Forma, Fusion, And Flow Industry Clouds
AUTODESK, INC.
Autodesk previewed new agentic AI across its three industry clouds: Autodesk Forma for Architecture, Engineering, and Construction; Autodesk Fusion for Design and Manufacturing; and Autodesk Flow for Media and Entertainment. These new capabilities are shaping the next generation of Autodesk Assistant, extending Autodesk's agentic AI experience across products, projects, and teams rather than inside a single tool, and drawing on connected project data to understand not just the question being asked, but the project behind it. Autodesk Assistant is generally available across many Autodesk products, including Fusion, Forma, and Flow, where it helps customers work with Autodesk AI inside the tools they already use.
The next-generation experience extends beyond any single product. The next-generation experience is designed to connect project intelligence with the right Autodesk capabilities across products, projects, and teams, including through a standalone experience planned for 2027. This next-generation Assistant is built around three priorities: Understand what needs attention.
Personal Pulse surfaces prioritized issues and insights across projects. Assistant Spaces gives teams and their agents a focused environment to investigate a problem, collaborate on it, and see its downstream effects. Act across workflows.
Assistant brings Autodesk's specialized design, engineering, and creative AI together with the precise capabilities professionals rely on to simulate, manufacture, and produce their work, turning intent into trusted, reviewable outcomes through natural-language and voice interaction. Bring your own intelligence. Assistant Builder lets customers connect their own AI agents, tools and trusted partner services to Autodesk project context, with support planned for third-party agents from the Design & Make Marketplace.
Behind the experience, Autodesk AI Orchestrator evaluates models based on the needs of a particular task, including accuracy, speed, security, and cost, allowing Autodesk to draw on different forms of intelligence rather than relying on a single model for every problem. Autodesk Assistant is grounded in actual project context and, like every Autodesk AI capability, is evaluated for data integrity, privacy and risk. Autodesk publishes AI Transparency Cards for Autodesk Assistant, covering the data and technologies used, safeguards, and known limitations.
Autodesk Assistant is designed to support professional judgment, with appropriate controls and human oversight. Autodesk Assistant is already available within Autodesk industry clouds and across many Autodesk products, including Fusion, Forma, and Flow. Autodesk is previewing the expanded next-generation experience at AU 2026.
The next-generation experience is not yet generally available. Availability, rollout timing, subscription terms, and regional details for these next-generation capabilities will be announced in 2027.

Autodesk names Diana Colella to lead architecture, engineering and construction business
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT 3 min read
Proven product leader to advance Forma industry cloud and AI strategy and drive the next phase of AEC growth
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ: ADSK) today announced that Diana Colella has been named executive vice president of its architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) business. Colella succeeds Amy Bunszel, who previously announced her retirement and will remain with Autodesk through November 2, 2026, to support the transition.
Colella will lead Autodesk's largest industry business as the company enters its next phase of growth in AEC, driven by Autodesk Forma, the company's industry cloud for AEC that connects data, context and workflows to deliver AI and project intelligence across the AEC lifecycle.
"The AEC industry is entering a new era, as AI creates new possibilities for how buildings and infrastructure are designed, built and operated," said Andrew Anagnost, president and CEO of Autodesk. "Amy and the AEC team have built a strong business and laid the foundation for the next phase of growth, with Forma becoming the industry cloud for AEC and AI helping customers navigate increasing complexity across the project lifecycle. Diana is the right leader for this moment. She brings a proven track record of leading through major technology shifts, aligning products, data and teams behind a clear vision, and turning innovation into tangible customer outcomes. Combined with her deep understanding of Autodesk and the industries we serve, Diana is uniquely positioned to build on this momentum and help shape the future of AEC."
In her new role, Colella will advance the Forma strategy while continuing to evolve our desktop products such as Revit and Civil 3D while connecting them more closely to Forma workflows. By bringing together the data and context created across the project lifecycle, Autodesk aims to make AI more useful in the work customers do every day, helping teams reduce friction, make better-informed decisions and increase their capacity to design and build.
Colella brings nearly three decades of Autodesk leadership experience spanning finance, strategy, sales, operations, product management and industry leadership. She joined Autodesk through the acquisition of Discreet Logic and has since held leadership roles across the company, including leading Autodesk's AutoCAD business and helping launch One AutoCAD. Her broad experience has given her deep insight into how Autodesk's products, operations and go-to-market teams work together to create customer success.
Most recently, Colella led the AI transformation of Autodesk's Media & Entertainment (M&E) business, where she advanced the Flow platform strategy and expanded Autodesk's role across the production lifecycle. Through acquisitions including Moxion, PIX and Wonder Dynamics, and the continued development of Autodesk Flow Studio, she helped broaden the value Autodesk delivers to creators and studios. Colella will continue to oversee the M&E business and will open a search for a new leader, reporting directly to her.
"Our customers are being asked to deliver more while navigating greater complexity, persistent resource constraints and rapid technological change," said Colella. "My priority is to listen to them, build on the strong foundation Amy and the team have created, and make sure the work we're doing across Forma and AI translates into meaningful improvements in how projects are designed, built and operated. I'm honored to lead Autodesk's AEC business at such an important moment for our customers and the industry."
The world's designers, engineers, builders, and creators trust Autodesk to help them design and make anything. From the buildings we live and work in, to the cars we drive and the bridges we drive over. From the products we use and rely on, to the movies and games that inspire us. Autodesk's Design and Make Platform unlocks the power of data to accelerate insights and automate processes, empowering customers with the technology to create the world around us and deliver better outcomes for their businesses and the planet. For more information, visit autodesk.com or follow @autodesk. #MakeAnything

"The AEC industry is entering a new era, as AI creates new possibilities for how buildings and infrastructure are designed, built and operated," said Andrew Anagnost, president and CEO of Autodesk. "Amy and the AEC team have built a strong business and laid the foundation for the next phase of growth, with Forma becoming the industry cloud for AEC and AI helping customers navigate increasing complexity across the project lifecycle. Diana is the right leader for this moment. She brings a proven track record of leading through major technology shifts, aligning products, data and teams behind a clear vision, and turning innovation into tangible customer outcomes. Combined with her deep understanding of Autodesk and the industries we serve, Diana is uniquely positioned to build on this momentum and help shape the future of AEC."
p>In her new role, Colella will advance the Forma strategy while continuing to evolve our desktop products such as Revit and Civil 3D while connecting them more closely to Forma workflows. By bringing together the data and context created across the project lifecycle, Autodesk aims to make AI more useful in the work customers do every day, helping teams reduce friction, make better-informed decisions and increase their capacity to design and build.
Colella brings nearly three decades of Autodesk leadership experience spanning finance, strategy, sales, operations, product management and industry leadership. She joined Autodesk through the acquisition of Discreet Logic and has since held leadership roles across the company, including leading Autodesk's AutoCAD business and helping launch One AutoCAD. Her broad experience has given her deep insight into how Autodesk's products, operations and go-to-market teams work together to create customer success.
Most recently, Colella led the AI transformation of Autodesk's Media & Entertainment (M&E) business, where she advanced the Flow platform strategy and expanded Autodesk's role across the production lifecycle. Through acquisitions including Moxion, PIX and Wonder Dynamics, and the continued development of Autodesk Flow Studio, she helped broaden the value Autodesk delivers to creators and studios. Colella will continue to oversee the M&E business and will open a search for a new leader, reporting directly to her.
"Our customers are being asked to deliver more while navigating greater complexity, persistent resource constraints and rapid technological change," said Colella. "My priority is to listen to them, build on the strong foundation Amy and the team have created, and make sure the work we're doing across Forma and AI translates into meaningful improvements in how projects are designed, built and operated. I'm honored to lead Autodesk's AEC business at such an important moment for our customers and the industry."

Autodesk's real bet at AU 2026 isn't a product. It's an assistant that knows the project | iTWire Skip to content
Autodesk's real bet at AU 2026 isn't a product. It's an assistant that knows the project
Every AI story at Autodesk University this year eventually comes back to the same argument: capacity, not ideas, is the constraint holding architecture, engineering, construction, manufacturing, and entertainment back. Especially if you look at the Australian stats from the State of Design and Make report. CEO Andrew Anagnost has been making that case for two years running. What is new at AU 2026 is the thing Autodesk is pointing to as the mechanism for unlocking it, the next generation of Autodesk Assistant.
If you have used Autodesk software recently, you've already met an earlier version of Assistant, a conversational helper sitting inside Fusion, Forma or Flow, answering questions, and taking a few tasks off your plate. That version is still there, and it is not going anywhere. What Autodesk previewed this week is something more ambitious, an agentic AI experience designed to work across products, projects, and teams rather than staying locked inside whichever tool you happen to have open.
Why this is not just another chatbot It's worth being precise about what "agentic" means here because the word gets thrown around loosely. Autodesk's definition is AI that uses project context to help professionals understand, plan and take action toward an intended outcome, not simply answer a question.
In practice, that is the difference between an assistant you have to ask the right question, and one that already knows something needs your attention before you have thought to ask. Anagnost frames the underlying problem plainly: "The constraint in our industries has never been about ideas. It is capacity, and the next generation of Autodesk Assistant delivers project intelligence to unlock more of it. For Design and Make professionals, 'probably right' is wrong because their work has consequences in the real world."
That last line is doing a lot of work. A general-purpose AI model can reason across anything, but it does not know your building code, your manufacturing tolerances, your production schedule, or the history of decisions that got a project to where it is today. Autodesk's pitch is that its Assistant does, because it's grounded in what the company calls project intelligence: actionable insight built from connected project data, industry context, and more than four decades of Autodesk's own design and engineering expertise, not the open internet.
Three industry clouds, one intelligence layer The next-generation Assistant isn't a standalone product bolted onto Autodesk's existing tools. It sits across the company's three industry clouds, each connecting a different part of the design-and-build world:
Autodesk Forma: the industry cloud for architecture, engineering and construction, bringing planning, design, construction and operations data into one connected environment.
Autodesk Fusion: the industry cloud for design and manufacturing, connecting product design, engineering, manufacturing and production around shared product data.
Autodesk Flow: the industry cloud for media and entertainment, connecting creative teams, production data and AI across content creation.
Because Assistant draws on all three, it can follow a problem across boundaries that used to require a person to manually reconstruct context every time work moved from one team or tool to the next. Autodesk's own example is a structural change to a building: the next generation of Assistant can understand what that change affects downstream, fabrication, schedule, cost, construction sequencing, operations, and surface the specific Autodesk capabilities needed to deal with it, rather than just describing that a problem exists.
Marius Jablonskis, Digital Transformation Leader at Norconsult, put his finger on why that matters to an actual project team: "Project teams don't work in one tool or one part of a project, and the next generation of Autodesk Assistant reflects that. The potential is to bring the right project context into the workflow so teams can understand what needs attention and act on it more easily. We also see real value in being able to bring our own tools and intelligence into the experience alongside Autodesk's."
What it actually does Strip away the branding and the next-generation Assistant is built around three concrete priorities:
Understand what needs attention. Personal Pulse surfaces prioritised issues and insights across a person's project, so the things that matter do not get buried in a task list. Assistant Spaces gives teams, and their own AI agents, a focused environment to investigate a specific problem together and see its downstream effects before committing to a decision.
Act across workflows. Assistant brings Autodesk's specialised design, engineering, and creative AI together with the precise tools professionals already rely on, turning intent into a reviewable outcome through natural language or voice, rather than requiring someone to manually operate five different pieces of software to get there.
Bring your own intelligence. Assistant Builder lets customers connect their own AI agents, tools and trusted partner services directly into Autodesk's project context, with support planned for third-party agents through the new Design & Make Marketplace. Autodesk is not pretending it can build every capability a customer needs. Instead, it is positioning itself as the connective layer other tools plug into.
Behind all of it is the Autodesk AI Orchestrator, which chooses between different AI models for a given task based on accuracy, speed, security, and cost, rather than routing every problem through a single model. It is a quietly significant design choice: Autodesk is betting that no one model will ever be the right answer for everything from a natural-language site query to a structural engineering calculation, so the system picks its intelligence to fit the job.
What this looks like industry by industry Architecture, engineering, and construction. Inside Forma and Revit, Assistant helps architects explore more design options and cuts down on repetitive documentation work, while flagging project changes that need human attention rather than burying them in a drawing set. New AI-powered construction agents handle document search, submittal review, and bid processing, reducing the manual review load on already-stretched project teams.
Design and manufacturing. In Fusion, new AI capabilities automate repetitive design and manufacturing tasks, and a new agentic PLM (product lifecycle management) experience helps connect product data and decisions across teams who would otherwise be working from different versions of the truth. Assistant is also expanding into Inventor and Vault, meeting engineers inside the tools they already use daily rather than asking them to adopt something new.
Media and entertainment. In Flow, tools like Flow Studio let artists assemble characters and AI-generated worlds and then direct and refine them in an editable 3D environment, keeping creative control with the artist rather than handing it to the model. MotionMaker in Maya reduces repetitive animation work while leaving the final performance in human hands.
Operations. With MaintainX now part of Autodesk, the operational data an asset generates after it's built, equipment performance, maintenance history, failure patterns, can feed back into Assistant and inform not just how that asset is maintained, but how the next one is designed. It is the clearest expression of Autodesk's "closing the loop" idea: intelligence that does not stop accumulating the day a project is handed over.
The trust question, and the honest caveats None of this works if nobody trusts the output, and Autodesk is clearly aware of that. Every Autodesk AI capability, including Assistant, is evaluated for data integrity, privacy and risk, and the company publishes AI Transparency Cards covering the data and technologies behind Assistant, its safeguards, and its known limitations. Assistant is explicitly designed to support professional judgment rather than replace it, with human oversight built in rather than optional.
It is also worth being clear-eyed about timing. Autodesk Assistant itself is available today across many Autodesk products, including Fusion, Forma and Flow. The next-generation, cross-product experience being previewed at AU 2026 is not yet generally available. Availability, rollout timing, subscription terms, and regional details are slated to be announced in 2027. This is a preview of direction, not a shipped product sitting on every desktop next week.
Why it matters beyond the keynote stage Autodesk's own 2027 State of Design & Make Report found that 70% of Design and Make leaders and experts surveyed expect AI to reduce mundane and repetitive work and free up capacity for the judgment, creativity, and ability their work requires. That is a consistent read across the industries Autodesk serves: professionals are not looking for AI to make the creative or technical calls. They are looking for it to clear away everything standing between them and making those calls well.
That is the real story behind the next generation of Autodesk Assistant. It is not a smarter chatbot. It's Autodesk trying to make the case that connected project data, industry-specific expertise and the right AI model for the right task, stitched together across its three industry clouds, can give design and make professionals back the one thing no amount of enthusiasm for AI has managed to create on its own: time.

Adobe (ADBE) vs. Autodesk (ADSK): Which AI-Hit Software Stock Has the Better Comeback?
Mon, October 5, 2026 at 8:48 PM PDT 5 min read
Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) and Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK) have something unusual in common. Both are excellent software companies that have been punished by investors for fears that artificial intelligence could make their products less valuable.
But the threat is not really the same.
Adobe's biggest problem is that AI can make it dramatically easier to create images, videos, designs, and documents. Some of the work that once required expensive professional software can now be done with a prompt.
Autodesk faces a different situation. Its software helps engineers, architects, manufacturers, and construction companies design things that eventually have to exist in the real world. AI can make those workflows faster, but it does not eliminate the need for precise engineering software.
Adobe ranks last in our list of 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. To see which stocks outranked it, click HERE.
Adobe (ADBE) vs. Autodesk (ADSK): Which AI-Hit Software Stock Has the Better Comeback?
Adobe has to prove that AI is a growth story, not a disruption story
Adobe's business is still remarkably strong.
Revenue grew 12% year over year in its latest quarter, while subscription revenue grew 14%. Adobe also crossed 1 billion monthly active users across its products. More importantly, its AI-first annual recurring revenue, or recurring revenue tied directly to newer AI products, surpassed $650 million and grew more than 150%.
The problem is that investors aren't convinced yet.
Adobe is increasingly giving users free access to products such as Firefly and Express in an effort to attract a much larger audience. That has helped push its creative freemium user base above 100 million, but it also means some users who might once have paid Adobe are now entering through a free funnel. Management expects the monetization of those users to show up later.
That is a risky bet. Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) needs AI to increase the value of its ecosystem faster than it reduces the value of the underlying software.
DON'T MISS: 12 High-Flying Stocks to Invest In
There are encouraging signs. Firefly, Adobe's generative AI platform, is being embedded into Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud products. Adobe is also building AI agents that can handle repetitive creative and marketing tasks rather than simply generate an image or paragraph.
But competitors are coming from every direction, from AI startups to cheaper creative tools. That is why the market has become so skeptical despite Adobe continuing to grow.
Autodesk's AI story is less flashy, but I think it may be easier to defend.
The company's software sits inside architecture, engineering, construction, and manufacturing workflows. These aren't just creative outputs. They are buildings, factories, machines and infrastructure.
That gives Autodesk something many AI companies do not have: context.
Autodesk is trying to connect design, construction, manufacturing and operations into one continuous flow of information. Its recent $3.6 billion acquisition of MaintainX is part of that strategy, bringing maintenance and operational data into the platform.
If Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ:ADSK) knows how something was designed, how it was built, and eventually how it performs in the real world, AI has much more useful information to work with.
Management calls this "project intelligence." In simpler terms, Autodesk wants to understand the entire life of an asset rather than just the design stage.
That could become a genuine competitive advantage.
The company's latest quarter showed that this isn't just an AI story on a slide. Revenue grew 16%, operating margins expanded, and management raised its full-year outlook.
So which stock is the better comeback?
This is where the valuation changes the answer.
Adobe is clearly the cheaper stock. At 8.73x forward earnings, the market is already assuming that its growth will slow and that AI will put pressure on its traditional businesses.
Autodesk at 17.61x is asking investors to pay more for a company whose AI strategy arguably has fewer obvious ways to undermine its core franchise.
Autodesk's business story looks like a more compelling case.
The more complicated the physical world becomes, the more valuable precise design, engineering, and operational data could become. Autodesk is trying to make that data more useful with AI, rather than simply defending software against AI-generated alternatives. Its management argues that the combination of industry data, context and engineering expertise can create an advantage that gets stronger as more workflows connect.
Adobe has a much harder job. It has to convince investors that AI will expand the creative economy enough to offset the possibility that AI also makes creative software easier to replace.
That said, Adobe shouldn't be dismissed at this valuation.
If its free users eventually convert into paying customers, while Firefly, Acrobat AI and its enterprise AI products become meaningful sources of incremental revenue, 8.73x forward earnings could look almost absurdly cheap in hindsight.
Adobe is much cheaper, but that alone does not make it the better buy. Autodesk trades at 17.61x forward earnings, which does not look expensive if its AI strategy and broader platform start paying off. Adobe has more room for upside if AI turns out to strengthen its business, but Autodesk may have the stronger position to defend.
According to Insider Monkey's database, 81 hedge funds held Adobe in Q2, down from 86 in Q1, while the value of their positions fell from about $5.70 billion to $4.14 billion. Autodesk saw a sharper decline in ownership, with 51 hedge funds holding the stock in Q2 versus 67 in Q1. The value of those positions also dropped from $3.17 billion to $2.28 billion.
While we acknowledge the potential of ADBE and ADSK as investments, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Mon, October 5, 2026 at 4:57 AM PDT 1 min read
Chart with green arrow going up ©Adobe Stock Images
Autodesk (NASDAQ:ADSK) shares rose 3.8% in pre-market trading after Schneider Electric announced an agreement to acquire PTC for $22.6 billion in cash.
Under the transaction, Schneider Electric will acquire PTC, a provider of industrial design and product lifecycle management software, at a 42.3% premium to its previous closing share price.
The acquisition is Schneider Electric's largest to date and provides a transaction benchmark for the industrial and engineering software sector, where Autodesk also operates.
Autodesk Expands AI Capabilities Across Fusion Products
The share-price move follows several recent product developments at Autodesk, including the wider rollout of Autodesk Assistant across its Fusion product portfolio.
At Autodesk University 2026, the company announced that Autodesk Assistant was generally available across the suite, extending natural-language, agentic AI capabilities to products including Inventor, Moldflow and Vault.
Flex token access for AI-powered workflows is scheduled to begin on October 6.
Infrastructure consultancy Arcadis has also expanded its AI collaboration with Autodesk, covering the use of Autodesk technology in construction and data-led project delivery.
Recent Quarter Shows Revenue and Profit Growth
Autodesk's pre-market advance came as the broader US equity market recorded smaller moves. The S&P 500 was up 0.1%, while the Nasdaq was broadly unchanged.
The Nasdaq reached a record intraday high on Friday.
Autodesk reported revenue growth of 16% in its most recent quarter, while net income increased 57%.
The Schneider Electric transaction for PTC has brought further attention to valuations in the engineering and industrial software sector, contributing to the pre-market move in Autodesk shares.

How Low Can Autodesk (ADSK) Stock Go?
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 11:44 AM PDT 3 min read
Autodesk (ADSK) stock has lost 22% over the past month following its recent earnings release, outstripping declines in peers such as Bentley Systems (down 16.4%) while the S&P 500 barely moved. If you own the shares, the worry now is a market-wide sell-off landing on top of that loss. So how low could Autodesk stock go if the whole market turns?
Autodesk Stock Has Usually Fallen Further Than The Market
In past market shocks, Autodesk stock has usually fallen further than the S&P 500. Autodesk stock has traded through 15 such shocks since 2007. On average, the stock fell 24.9% from peak to trough during each shock, compared to 15.8% for the index.
Its deepest fall came in the 2008-2009 financial crisis. The stock lost 77% then, against 53% for the S&P 500. No fall in its full price history has been deeper. In the 2022 inflation shock, as the Fed raised rates, the stock fell 42%, against 24% for the index.
After each fall, the stock took a median of 2.7 months to climb from its low back to its old high. Two recoveries took more than a year, though. After the 2022 fall, the stock needed 28 months to return. Autodesk has changed a great deal in the past five years.
How Has Autodesk Changed In Five Years?
Autodesk is now a larger and more profitable business. Its debt is low. Its revenue over the past twelve months was $7.8 billion, against $4.0 billion five years earlier. Autodesk's debt equals 8.7% of its market value, against 20.7% for the S&P 500.
Its operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, has risen every year for three years. It now stands at 27.9%, up from 19.4% three years ago. That is its highest level in ten years.
Autodesk's sales depend heavily on one part of the business. Its largest reported segment, Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations, brought in $3.6 billion in fiscal 2026. That was half of all revenue that year.
Management said on the fiscal Q2 2027 call that its construction business, part of that segment, is growing by more than 20%. Management also said that growth comes from how little the construction industry uses technology, not from cyclical macroeconomic indicators. Management built its outlook on the economy staying broadly stable through the year.
How Much Could Autodesk Alone Cost Your Portfolio?
Suppose your Autodesk shares are a tenth of your portfolio. Now picture the stock falling 77% from today's price, as deep as its 2008-2009 fall. On its own, that holding would take 7.7% off your whole portfolio, with everything else held flat. At a fifth of your portfolio, they would take 15.4%. The wait could be long, too. After the 2009 low, the stock took 58 months to get back to its old high.
You would need to sit through that wait as well as the loss. Whether Autodesk avoids another severe drawdown will depend heavily on whether construction software adoption can truly outpace an economic downturn, rather than slowing with it.
Beyond ADSK: A Systematic Way To Grow Your Money

Since its inception, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has returned 105%, beating the benchmark that combines the three major indices - the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap, and Russell 2000. And it did so without taking the concentrated risk that comes with do-it-yourself stock picking.

Autodesk (ADSK) stock has fallen 23% since late August. A $10,000 holding bought at the high is now worth about $7,700. A fall that fast pulls you toward buying, but the shares still cost more than the market on earnings. The reason to buy is that past Autodesk drops this deep mostly paid off, and the business is still sound.
Why Did Autodesk Stock Fall After A Strong Quarter?
News reports tie the start of the fall to a profit outlook that disappointed, even though the quarter itself beat. The shares peaked on August 27, the day Autodesk reported its fiscal second-quarter results. Revenue and earnings per share both came in above the top of management's own guide.
Those reports said investors focused instead on a third-quarter adjusted profit forecast below Wall Street's estimates. Reuters added that investors worry about possible disruption from AI tools.
Autodesk's own price history shows how earlier drops like this one ended. Here, a dip means a fall of 20% or more within 30 trading days. For example, a $100 share that slides to $80 inside that window would count. Autodesk's latest fall is as deep as the drops in that record, so the record applies here.
Autodesk Dip Buyers Mostly Came Out Ahead
Most buyers of past Autodesk dips were ahead a year later. Not counting this drop, the stock had 11 dips since 2010, though the latest two are too recent to judge. Of the other nine, 7 ended the following year higher. The median return over that year was 26%, so half did better and half did worse.
Collecting that gain meant sitting through more losses first. After past dips, the stock fell a median of a further 12% before it turned. The median best gain within the year was 51%. It took a median of 307 days, about ten months, to get there.
Those results come from Autodesk's past, so they only help if the company under today's drop is still in good shape.
Is Autodesk's Business Still Sound Under The Drop?
Autodesk's business is sound, but you still pay more than the market for it. Revenue grew 17.9% over the past twelve months, faster than its three-year average of 14.4% a year. Its largest segment, Architecture, Engineering, Construction and Operations, grew 22% in fiscal 2026.
Autodesk also keeps more of each sale than the market as a whole. Its operating margin, the share of revenue left after its costs, was 28%, against 18.6% for the S&P 500. Operating cash flow came to 37% of revenue over the past year.
The price is the catch. Autodesk trades at 33.1 times its past year's earnings, against 22.1 for the S&P 500. So you pay about 50% more for each dollar of Autodesk's profit than for the market's.
Profit is also where the one complication shows up. In August, management raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook, which now includes MaintainX, a company Autodesk has already acquired. Management also lowered its guide for the operating margin under standard accounting to 25% to 27%, from 27%. Management said the MaintainX acquisition dilutes margins.
Autodesk's next report is expected in late November. For the fiscal third quarter, management guided adjusted earnings per share of $3.04 to $3.09.
The reason to buy Autodesk now needs the record to repeat and the business to hold up. Adjusted earnings per share below that range in November would break the business half of it. A result inside or above the range would leave it standing for now. Even a buyer who is right should expect the stock to fall further first. After past dips, the median further fall was 12%.

Design Software Stocks Q2 In Review: Autodesk (NASDAQ:ADSK) Vs Peers
Design Software Stocks Q2 In Review: Autodesk (NASDAQ:ADSK) Vs Peers
Earnings results often indicate what direction a company will take in the months ahead. With Q2 behind us, let's have a look at Autodesk (NASDAQ:ADSK) and its peers.
The demand for rich, interactive 2D, 3D, VR and AR experiences is growing, and while the ubiquitous metaverse might still be more of a buzzword than a real thing, what is real is the demand for the tools to create these experiences, whether they are games, 3D tours or interactive movies.
The 7 design software stocks we track reported a strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 1.2% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 2.2% above.
In light of this news, share prices of the companies have held steady as they are up 2.9% on average since the latest earnings results.
Starting with AutoCAD in the 1980s and evolving into a comprehensive design ecosystem, Autodesk (NASDAQ:ADSK) provides software solutions for architecture, engineering, construction, manufacturing, and entertainment industries to design, simulate, and visualize projects.
Autodesk reported revenues of $2.05 billion, up 16.1% year on year. This print exceeded analysts' expectations by 1.7%. Overall, it was a satisfactory quarter for the company with an impressive beat of analysts' annual recurring revenue estimates but EPS guidance for next quarter missing analysts' expectations.
"AI turns connected data and context into actionable project intelligence that can ease endemic capacity constraints, raise the bar on what's possible in the physical world, and help our customers do more with scarce resources," said Andrew Anagnost, CEO of Autodesk. "To realize that promise, customers need AI that is accurate, fast enough to stay in the flow of work, and affordable enough to use every day. The future of AI for the built world will belong to the trusted platform that combines the richest context with the right models to deliver the best outcomes for customers. Autodesk is uniquely positioned because we build project intelligence across the asset lifecycle by converging design, make, and operate through a continuous flow of data, context, and experience."
Even though it had a relatively good quarter, the market seems discontent with the results. The stock is down 19.9% since reporting and currently trades at $216.68.

Powering over half of the world's mobile games and expanding into industries from automotive to architecture, Unity (NYSE:U) provides software tools and services that allow developers to create, run, and monetize interactive 2D and 3D content across multiple platforms.
Unity reported revenues of $546.5 million, up 23.9% year on year, outperforming analysts' expectations by 6.1%. The business had a stunning quarter with an impressive beat of analysts' billings estimates and EBITDA guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations.
Unity pulled off the biggest analyst estimate beat in the group. The market seems happy with the results as the stock is up 30.8% since reporting. It currently trades at $46.40.
Is now the time to buy Unity? Access our full analysis of the earnings results here, it's free.
Originally known as Parametric Technology Corporation until its 2013 rebranding, PTC (NASDAQ:PTC) provides software that helps manufacturers design, develop, and service physical products through digital solutions for CAD, PLM, ALM, and SLM.
PTC reported revenues of $600 million, down 6.8% year on year, falling short of analysts' expectations by 1.3%. It was a slower quarter as it posted a significant miss of analysts' billings estimates and a miss of analysts' annual recurring revenue estimates.
PTC delivered the slowest revenue growth and weakest full-year guidance update among its peers. Interestingly, the stock is up 7.7% since the results and currently trades at $142.67.
Read our full analysis of PTC's results here.
Powering the chips behind everything from smartphones to AI accelerators for over 35 years, Cadence Design Systems (NASDAQ:CDNS) provides essential computational software, hardware, and intellectual property used by engineers to design and verify advanced electronic systems and semiconductors.
Cadence Design Systems reported revenues of $1.58 billion, up 24.2% year on year. This result topped analysts' expectations by 0.5%. It was a very strong quarter as it also logged a solid beat of analysts' billings estimates and EPS guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations.
Cadence Design Systems delivered the fastest revenue growth and highest full-year guidance raise of the whole group. The stock is down 8.4% since reporting and currently trades at $310.00.
Read our full, actionable report on Cadence Design Systems here, it's free.
Known for its iconic "D" logo that appears before countless movies and TV shows, Dolby Laboratories (NYSE:DLB) designs and licenses audio and video technologies that enhance entertainment experiences in movies, TV shows, music, and other media.
Dolby Laboratories reported revenues of $305 million, down 3.3% year on year. This print lagged analysts' expectations by 2%. Zooming out, it was a mixed quarter as it also produced revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations but EPS guidance for next quarter meeting analysts' expectations.
Dolby Laboratories pulled off the highest guidance raise but had the weakest performance against analyst estimates in the group. The stock is up 12.1% since reporting and currently trades at $58.04.
Read our full, actionable report on Dolby Laboratories here, it's free.
Over the past year, investors have been forced to repeatedly answer the same question: what is the market's biggest risk? The answer has changed several times, and each shift has reshaped market leadership.
Late in 2025 and early 2026, artificial intelligence became the market's primary uncertainty. Investors questioned whether AI would erode software pricing power and weaken competitive moats as AI made it easier to replicate once-differentiated products.
By the spring, technology took a back seat to geopolitics. The U.S. conflict with Iran briefly became the market's dominant narrative, raising concerns about oil prices, inflation, and global growth. But as energy markets remained orderly and fears of a prolonged supply disruption faded, investors quickly turned their focus back to fundamentals.

Autodesk names Diana Colella to lead architecture, engineering and construction business
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT 3 min read
Proven product leader to advance Forma industry cloud and AI strategy and drive the next phase of AEC growth
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Autodesk, Inc. (NASDAQ: ADSK) today announced that Diana Colella has been named executive vice president of its architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) business. Colella succeeds Amy Bunszel, who previously announced her retirement and will remain with Autodesk through November 2, 2026, to support the transition.
Colella will lead Autodesk's largest industry business as the company enters its next phase of growth in AEC, driven by Autodesk Forma, the company's industry cloud for AEC that connects data, context and workflows to deliver AI and project intelligence across the AEC lifecycle.
"The AEC industry is entering a new era, as AI creates new possibilities for how buildings and infrastructure are designed, built and operated," said Andrew Anagnost, president and CEO of Autodesk. "Amy and the AEC team have built a strong business and laid the foundation for the next phase of growth, with Forma becoming the industry cloud for AEC and AI helping customers navigate increasing complexity across the project lifecycle. She brings a proven track record of leading through major technology shifts, aligning products, data and teams behind a clear vision, and turning innovation into tangible customer outcomes. Combined with her deep understanding of Autodesk and the industries we serve, Diana is uniquely positioned to build on this momentum and help shape the future of AEC." In her new role, Colella will advance the Forma strategy while continuing to evolve our desktop products such as Revit and Civil 3D while connecting them more closely to Forma workflows. By bringing together the data and context created across the project lifecycle, Autodesk aims to make AI more useful in the work customers do every day, helping teams reduce friction, make better-informed decisions and increase their capacity to design and build. Colella brings nearly three decades of Autodesk leadership experience spanning finance, strategy, sales, operations, product management and industry leadership. She joined Autodesk through the acquisition of Discreet Logic and has since held leadership roles across the company, including leading Autodesk's AutoCAD business and helping launch One AutoCAD. Expedia Makes Flying Easier with One Key Benefits: Lounge Access During Delays, Less Time at Airport Security and Money Back When Fares Drop
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT 11 min read
SEATTLE, October 06, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Expedia® today introduced new Expedia One Key benefits designed to make travel easier from booking to boarding, giving travelers immediate value and savings, while helping them earn rewards for future trips. Expedia One Key is Expedia's free loyalty program, offering instant member discounts and OneKeyCash™ rewards that can be used on future eligible travel.
Expedia One Key's updated benefits include:
Free lounge access for delayed flights: Expedia is expanding free lounge access for delayed flights to eligible Gold and Platinum One Key™ members.
Discounted CLEAR+ membership and CLEAR Concierge services: Travelers can speed through airport security and get to their gate faster.
Price Drop Protection: If the price of an eligible booked flight drops before departure, Expedia automatically provides the fare difference in OneKeyCash™.
Instant Savings, while earning OneKeyCash: Expedia One Key members can enjoy instant discounts with Member Prices, plus earn 1% to 3% back in OneKeyCash to use on future travel.
"Travelers told us they want a loyalty program with rewards and perks program that delivers real savings right away while helping them earn rewards for future trips," said Casey Lehman, Vice President of Loyalty, Expedia Group. "We wanted to make our loyalty program simpler for our members, so we're strengthening our proposition of instant discounts plus rewards for future trips, while adding distinctive travel perks that support members from booking to boarding—including lounge access during delays, less time at airport security through our CLEAR partnership and OneKeyCash when a flight price drops."
What is new with Expedia One Key loyalty benefits?
Expedia One Key comes with two ways to save: instant discounts with Member Prices, plus OneKeyCash to use on future travel. With a new "1-2-3" path to earn, members can start seeing value immediately and build toward even greater savings, OneKeyCash and travel perks as they progress through the program.
OneKeyCash remains flexible: every $1 in OneKeyCash is worth $1 toward eligible bookings across hotels, vacation homes, cars and activities—with no blackout dates.
How does free lounge access for delayed flights work for Expedia One Key members?
Expedia is enhancing its free lounge access benefit for delayed flights and extending eligibility to Gold members. Eligible members whose flight is delayed by 90 minutes or more can receive complimentary access to an airport lounge or other eligible airport experience. The benefit will initially operate as a pilot as Expedia continues to enhance the experience and evaluate member engagement. [1]
Eligible passes provide access to lounges in the LoungeKey network, including independent operators such as The Club, Escape Lounges, Plaza Premium, and Aspire. The benefit may also include participating airport bars and restaurants, spas, gaming lounges, and sleep pods. If no lounge or alternative option is available at the airport, each eligible passenger on the same itinerary receives $20 in OneKeyCash.
According to a recent consumer survey, almost half of U.S. travelers (48%) have experienced a flight delay of 90 minutes or more, while 54.1% find airport security stressful, including 12.3% who find it very stressful. Expedia customer feedback shows that providing eligible travelers with QR-enabled access to an in-terminal lounge can turn a frustrating disruption into a more comfortable experience.
What are the CLEAR Partnership benefits available to Expedia One Key members?
Through the CLEAR partnership, Expedia One Key members can access preferred pricing and services designed to make the airport experience more seamless. The CLEAR partnership gives U.S. One Key members access to tier-based discounts on CLEAR+ and CLEAR Concierge to help travelers have secure, stress-free experiences—from home to gate and back again.
Members can sign up for discounted CLEAR+ products through Expedia to move through security faster at more than 60 U.S. airports using secure identity verification. CLEAR Concierge provides a dedicated Ambassador to help guide travelers from the curb to their gate when they need an extra set of hands at the airport.
Through Expedia:
Platinum members: CLEAR+ annual Membership for $129. A Membership plus two CLEAR Concierge Departure Service bookings for $199.
Gold and Silver members: CLEAR+ annual Membership for $179. A Membership, plus two CLEAR Concierge Departure Service bookings for $249.
Blue members: CLEAR+ annual Membership for $209.
Silver, Gold and Platinum members: 20% off additional CLEAR Concierge Departure Service bookings.
Airport security is a meaningful source of stress, and travelers say they would use time saved at security for practical and enjoyable parts of the airport experience. According to the consumer survey: [2]
"Walk through security instantly" was selected by 23.2% as their preferred airport superpower, nearly as popular as automatic upgrades at 23.9%.
The time problem is tangible: The average typical security wait is 22.1 minutes. 44.3% usually wait at least 20 minutes, and 19.8% usually wait 30 minutes or more. Separately, 30.0% report that their longest-ever security wait was at least 60 minutes.
What is Expedia's One Key Price Drop Protection and how does it help me save money on flights?
Gold and Platinum members who book eligible flights in the Expedia app can receive free One Key Price Drop Protection. If the price drops before departure, Expedia automatically provides the difference in OneKeyCash.
After booking an eligible flight in the Expedia app and until the day the flight is scheduled to depart, Expedia automatically checks the price of the flight on Expedia once every 24 hours. Price checks are based on the flight details booked. Expedia will send notifications about any price changes. If the price of the eligible flight drops on Expedia, the traveler will get a Price Drop Protection Payment in OneKeyCash for the difference after the trip is completed.
In 2025, Expedia gave $28 million in OneKeyCash directly to Gold and Platinum One Key members through its Price Drop Protection program. [3]
How do members progress through One Key tiering status?
Members continue to advance through tiers by collecting trip elements as they travel—not simply by completing bookings. Members join as Blue, reach Silver after five trip elements, Gold after 15 and Platinum after 30. That means a new member can reach Silver after a single trip, such as two hotel nights and a three-day car rental. By recognizing the individual components of a journey, One Key gives members more ways to make progress toward higher status.
The program's tiered instant discounts remain available across a wide selection of hotels, car rentals and activities. The new earn structure replaces the previous flat 2% rate with a clearer, tiered approach:
Blue: 10% or more in instant discounts, plus 1% back in OneKeyCash
Silver: 15% or more in instant discounts, plus 2% back in OneKeyCash
Gold: 20% or more in instant discounts, plus 2% back in OneKeyCash
Platinum: 20% or more in instant discounts, plus 3% back in OneKeyCash
At the highest tier, Platinum members now earn One Key's highest standard rate—3% back in OneKeyCash—helping them build toward their next trip faster.
What rewards do One Key Credit Cardholders earn?
The One Key Credit Card delivers value on every trip and beyond, giving cardholders 3% back in OneKeyCash on Expedia bookings made with the card, including flights, plus an additional 3% for Silver Members, 4% for Gold Members and 6% for Platinum Members when booking VIP Access properties—up to 9% back on eligible VIP Expedia bookings.
Cardholders also earn 3% back on gas, groceries and dining, as well as 1.5% back everywhere else with the no-annual-fee card or 2% back with the Fee Card, making it easy to earn rewards on everyday purchases both within and beyond Expedia.
What else is changing for Expedia One Key members?
Expedia is simplifying or retiring selected lower-value and legacy features while investing in benefits designed to deliver more noticeable value.
Standalone flights no longer earn the previous 0.2% in OneKeyCash through the loyalty program.
Flights still count as an eligible trip element toward tier status.
Members can continue to use OneKeyCash on eligible flight bookings as before.
Package bookings earn OneKeyCash on the non-flight portions of the trip.
The Hotel Price Guarantee benefit is being sunset for new bookings.
Q: What happens if an eligible flight is delayed by 90 minutes or more?
A: Eligible U.S. One Key Gold and Platinum members and additional travelers on the same itinerary can receive complimentary access to an airport lounge or other eligible airport experience through Expedia, subject to the benefit terms.
Q: When must a flight be registered for complimentary lounge access?
A: Flights must be registered at least 24 hours before scheduled departure, and certain airlines are excluded.
Q: What happens if no lounge or alternative airport experience is available?
A: Each eligible passenger on the same itinerary receives $20 in OneKeyCash, subject to the benefit terms.
Q: What lounges are included as part of the complimentary lounge access benefit?
A. Eligible passes provide access to lounges in the LoungeKey network, including independent operators such as The Club, Escape Lounges, Plaza Premium, and Aspire. The benefit may also include participating airport bars and restaurants, spas, gaming lounges, and sleep pods; major airline-branded lounges are generally excluded.
Q: Why do travelers value lounge access during flight delays?
A: Among travelers who have experienced a flight delay, 83.0% consider a delay-related benefit valuable, and 30.5% prefer an airport lounge as a place to wait during a delay of 90 minutes or more.
Q: What is CLEAR+?
A: CLEAR+ is an annual Membership that enables Members to move through security faster at more than 60 U.S. airports using secure identity verification.
Q: What is CLEAR Concierge?
A: CLEAR Concierge provides a dedicated Ambassador to help guide travelers from curb to gate.
Q: Who can access CLEAR benefits through Expedia?
A: U.S. One Key members can access CLEAR+ pricing and CLEAR Concierge options through Expedia based on their One Key status.
Q: What is Expedia One Key?
A: Expedia One Key is Expedia Group's free travel rewards program in the U.S., shared across Expedia, Hotels.com® and Vrbo®. Members receive Member Prices discounts, earn OneKeyCash on eligible bookings and share tier status across participating brands.
Q: How much is OneKeyCash worth?
A: One dollar in OneKeyCash is equal to one dollar to spend on eligible travel, with no blackout dates.
Q: Do flights still count toward One Key status?
A: Yes. An eligible one-way or round-trip flight ticket continues to count as one trip element toward status. Expedia One Key Credit Card holders can also earn OneKeyCash when purchasing their flight on the credit card. However, standalone airfare no longer earns the previous 0.2% in OneKeyCash through the loyalty program.
Q: What happens to OneKeyCash on package bookings?
A: Package bookings earn OneKeyCash on the non-flight portions of the trip.
